prompt.context: Minerva's University Fluids Research Lab has discovered a more efficient way to transport crude petroleum oil inside pipelines. This new technology can be used in midstream applications where the oil is acquired from the extraction plant and delivered to the refinery plant. The university invested $1,200M in this project during the last 12 years. The new technology mixes water and oil under certain conditions to reduce the loss of energy caused by the friction between the oil and the pipeline surface while being transported. As a result, the transport between two given points gets 15% faster and the useful lifetime of the pipelines increases by 20%.
prompt.question: Minerva's University asked our help to determine the value at which they should sell the technology. What price would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors and what is their market share?
clarifying_info.a: National Oil Company (NOC) is the only player. However, the market is open for the last two years.
Primarily NOC. However, two other prospects are interested in entering the market.

clarifying_info.q: Does the University have a patent? How long does it last?
clarifying_info.a: The University has already filed for a patent, which lasts for 20 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is NOC's current pipeline capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Full capacity. Surplus is transported by more expensive means such as rail car, barge, and truck.

clarifying_info.q: How is the demand for crude oil?
clarifying_info.a: NOC sells all the crude oil it buys. See Exhibit 2 for the next years' forecast.

clarifying_info.q: Can NOC build more pipelines to substitute other means of transportation?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, it is an alternative. However, there are costs involved. Additional capacity: 50,000 barrels per day; time to implement: 2 years; cost per additional capacity unit: $700M.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to implement this technology?
clarifying_info.a: Minerva's University estimates that the technology would be running in 100% of the pipelines in one year at $2,000M installation cost.

exhibits.title: Income Statement and Cost of Sales Breakdown
exhibits.shows: Table 1 shows an income statement for Year 0 assuming sales of 2M barrels per day. Table 2 shows the cost of sales broken down by means of transportation, listing cost per barrel and share of total barrels for each mode.

exhibits.title: Crude Oil Demand Forecast
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing crude oil demand forecast in millions of barrels per day over 20 years. Demand rises linearly from 2M barrels/day at Year 1 to 2.5M barrels/day at Year 20.

data.note: In a given year, assume demand per day is the same for all 360 days.

framework: A) PRICING: Value = (1) Savings in cost of transportation + (2) Savings in cost of replacing pipelines - (3) Cost to implement
(1) Savings in cost of transportation: Increased pipeline speed raises delivery capacity, allowing volume currently shipped via expensive modes (truck, rail) to shift to cheaper pipeline
(2) Savings in cost of replacing pipelines: Extended pipeline lifetime reduces replacement frequency and associated capital expenditure
B) COMPARISON: Validate the price range by benchmarking against (4) Minerva's research investment ($1,200M floor) and (5) NOC's alternative of expanding the pipeline network ($7,000M ceiling)

questions.prompt: Calculate the Savings in Cost of Transportation (SCOT) over 20 years (the patent lifetime).
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize that (a) 15% speed increase lets the same pipeline carry more volume so some truck/rail volume shifts to pipeline, and (b) need to compute total barrels sold over 20 years using the trapezoid area of Exhibit 2, then multiply by the proportional cost saving from modal shift.

math.setup: SCOT = Total sales over 20 years × Savings per barrel from switching. Total sales = trapezoid area of demand chart × 360 days × $10/barrel. Savings per barrel = % shift to pipeline × (weighted premium vs pipeline).
steps: % increase in pipeline use = 15% speed increase × 70% currently on pipeline = 10.5% ≈ 10%

questions.prompt: Calculate the Savings in Cost of Replacing Pipelines (SCRP) over 20 years.
questions.guidance: The 20% lifetime increase means pipelines last 20% longer, so replacement cycles are fewer. Candidate should derive the current lifetime from Exhibit 1 data or given data, then compute the fraction of replacement cost saved.

math.setup: SCRP = Annual replacement cost × 20 years × (1 - new lifetime / current lifetime). Current lifetime = 5 years; new lifetime = 5 × 1.20 = 6 years → fraction saved = 1 - 5/6 = 1/6 but casebook uses 1 - 4/5 = 1/5 with lifetime going from 5 to 6 interpreted as saving 1 replacement cycle every 5: simplified as 1 - 4/5.
steps: Annual cost of replacing pipelines = $1,000M (from Exhibit 1)
Lifetime of regular pipeline = 5 years; new lifetime = ~6 years

questions.prompt: Calculate the net value of the technology to NOC (gross savings minus installation cost).
questions.guidance: Simple aggregation of the two savings streams minus the installation cost to arrive at the maximum NOC would rationally pay.

math.setup: Net value = SCOT + SCRP - Installation cost
math.answer: $8,000M — the ceiling price NOC would pay to guarantee positive savings

questions.prompt: What is the cost of NOC's alternative: expanding the pipeline network to eliminate reliance on other transport modes?
questions.guidance: Given data provides unit economics. Candidate must figure out how many expansion units are needed to cover the capacity gap (0.5M barrels/day) and multiply by unit cost.

math.setup: Total investment = (Additional capacity needed / Unit capacity) × Unit cost
math.answer: $7,000M — NOC would not pay more than this for the technology

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or sensitive assumptions could affect the recommended price or the technology's value?

categories.name: Implementation risks
ideas: Delay in installation beyond the one-year estimate
Technical failure or performance shortfall vs. the 15% speed / 20% lifetime claims

categories.name: Market & demand risks
ideas: Crude oil demand fluctuations due to economic crisis or energy transition
Oil price fluctuation affecting revenue per barrel — mitigated by futures contracts
Two new market entrants competing with NOC could alter negotiating leverage

categories.name: Geographic & logistical constraints
ideas: Some regions may only be reachable by specific transport modes, limiting the switchable volume
Not all 4,800 km of pipeline may be suitable for the water-oil mixing technology

categories.name: Financial risks
ideas: High upfront installation cost ($2,000M) requires NOC to arrange financing (cash surplus, bank loan, equity raise)
NOC may discount future savings at a high rate, reducing willingness to pay

categories.name: IP & competitive risks
ideas: Risk of reverse-engineering after 20-year patent expiry

recommendation: Sell the technology for a price of approximately $1,500M upfront plus a 30% participation in the additional revenue generated while the patent is in force (approximately $3,000M in royalties over 20 years), yielding total proceeds of ~$4,500M

The technology delivers ~$8,000M in net savings to NOC over 20 years (cost of transport savings $6,000M + pipeline lifetime savings $4,000M - installation $2,000M); any price below $8,000M is rational for NOC to accept
The price must exceed Minerva's $1,200M research investment to recover sunk costs; the reasonable negotiation range is therefore $1,200M to $7,000M (the alternative expansion cost)
The technology is superior to NOC's alternative pipeline expansion ($7,000M, 2-year lead time) on both cost and speed (1-year implementation)
risks: Delay in installation of the new technology beyond one year
Limitation in reaching some regions accessible only by a specific transport mode
High upfront installation cost ($2,000M) — NOC may need external financing
Crude oil price fluctuation — recommend futures contracts to lock in buying and selling prices
Demand fluctuations driven by macroeconomic crises or energy transition
next_steps: Verify savings calculations with NOC's own operational data and assumptions
Define a negotiation strategy based on the $1,200M floor and $7,000M ceiling
If negotiations with NOC fail, approach the two other market entrants as alternative buyers
Conduct due diligence on patent filing status and enforceability in Mexico
